The maximum total length attained by Boxlip mullet is 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], a value based on measurements of the largest individuals collected in the eastern Mediterranean. This species, a member of the family Mugilidae, exhibits a body shape typical of coastal mugilids, with a robust, fusiform form suited for rapid swimming in shallow, productive waters. Available data indicate that the total length at which sexual maturity, defined as the onset of puberty, is reached is 12.9 centimeters [Lp = 12.9 centimeters]. This relatively modest size at puberty, compared to the ultimate length, suggests a life history strategy that prioritises early reproductive investment, a pattern observed in several other small-bodied mullet species. The rapid attainment of maturity allows individuals to begin contributing to the next generation before facing the elevated mortality risks associated with larger body sizes in periodically disturbed coastal environments. These growth parameters are derived from extensive surveys of commercial catches and scientific trawls conducted along the Levantine coast, providing a robust empirical foundation for understanding the species' population dynamics and its role in local fisheries.

At a constant environmental temperature of 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of Boxlip mullet, expressed through its daily egg production, has been estimated. Detailed observations of captive females held under these thermal conditions, which reflect typical late-spring water temperatures in its native range, reveal that a single mature female can produce approximately 164 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 164 eggs per day]. This elevated daily output is characteristic of batch-spawning mugilids and is thought to maximise reproductive success by staggering gamete release over an extended spawning season. The value reported here is based on extrapolations from the congeneric species Planiliza parsia, scaled to the body size of Oedalechilus labeo. It represents an upper bound of reproductive potential under favourable laboratory conditions, likely exceeding rates achievable in the wild where resource availability and predation pressure act as significant constraints on fecundity and spawning frequency.

Female Boxlip mullet that have completed their somatic growth reach a maximum wet weight of 159.2 grams [Wwi = 159.2 grams], a value derived from a length-weight relationship calculated using the species' ultimate total length. This allometric equation, of the form W = aL^b, yields a robust estimate of asymptotic body mass, which is comparable to that of other small mullet species, such as Liza aurata. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty, corresponding to the onset of sexual maturation at the 12.9-centimeter length threshold, is 22.3 grams [Wwp = 22.3 grams]. The substantial increase in mass from puberty to the ultimate size—nearly a sevenfold difference—highlights the prolonged period of somatic growth that occurs after the onset of reproductive capability. This pattern suggests that Boxlip mullet allocate considerable energetic resources to increasing body size even after initiating reproduction, a life-history strategy that may enhance fecundity in later breeding seasons as larger females produce more eggs per spawning event.

The wet weight of a newly hatched Boxlip mullet larva, representing the initial body mass following yolk-sac absorption, has been estimated at 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams]. This remarkably small starting mass is consistent with the small egg diameter typical of the Mugilidae, which for this species is approximately 0.9 millimeters, based on data from the related flathead grey mullet Mugil cephalus. Such a minimal larval mass imposes a severe constraint on early-life survival by limiting the yolk reserves available to sustain the developing larva before it begins exogenous feeding. The transition to active feeding, occurring within a few days of hatching, is therefore a critical bottleneck in the species' life cycle. The tiny size also makes the larvae highly vulnerable to starvation and predation during the planktonic phase, factors that likely drive the high fecundity observed in adults as a compensatory mechanism for extremely low juvenile survival rates in the coastal environment.

Longevity in Boxlip mullet, as determined from mark-recapture studies and otolith ageing, reaches approximately ten years [am = approximately ten years] when individuals are reared under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C]. This lifespan is typical of small to medium-sized mugilids, which generally exhibit lifespans ranging from six to fifteen years depending on environmental conditions and predation regimes. The relationship between growth and lifespan in this species is notable: individuals achieve a substantial portion of their ultimate size within the first two to three years of life, after which growth decelerates markedly. The extended post-maturational period, spanning roughly seven years, allows for multiple annual spawning seasons, contributing to the species' overall reproductive output. This life-history pattern contrasts with that of short-lived, highly fecund fish that experience rapid senescence, suggesting that Boxlip mullet follows a more conservative strategy that balances gradual somatic investment with sustained, iteroparous reproduction across a moderately long adult lifespan.
